newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Chechnya massacre survivors give grisly testimony.
newsitem.headline: Chechnya massacre survivors give grisly testimony.

text.p: Survivors of the massacre of six Western staffers of the International Committee of the Red Cross gave a chilling account on Friday of 10 minutes of sheer horror in a hospital compound in Chechnya before dawn.

The six victims, five of them women, were shot dead in their sleep on Tuesday by a group of five or six masked men in military gear, wearing boots and carrying guns with silencers, the Geneva-based agency said in a statement of the first account of survivors.
Survivors said the gunmen entered the ICRC hospital compound in Novye Atagi village southwest of Grozny, the capital of the Russian breakaway region, at 3.30 a.m.
By the time they fled, leaving behind the dead including a nurse they met in a corridor and killed, it was 3.40 a.m.
The attackers forced the door of the hospital's administrative building open and fired shots at the door of a room where the safe was kept, but failed to get in.
They then stormed into the staff headquarters, where 18 expatriate ICRC employees and three Chechen employees were sleeping, in addition to two more expatriates in an annexe.

Fourteen staff members escaped death because they had locked their doors at bedtime. The gunmen tried in vain to break down the doors that were locked, then came across a nurse in the corridor preparing to go on duty and killed her, the ICRC said.

"The men systematically tried all the doors. They murdered five ICRC employees who had not locked themselves in, shooting them at point-blank range, the gun muzzles practically against their skin," the statement said.
The Swiss delegate who was in charge of the operation, Christophe Hensch, was wounded in the shoulder by a gunman who burst into his bedroom but survived by pretending he was dead.
The gunmen also threatened two Chechen employees but spared their lives after checking their identities, the statement said.
They escaped after a burst of automatic fire, probably from a guard in the area. The village military commander arrived at the scene at four a.m. with an armed escort.
"The attack clearly targetted ICRC expatriate staff. If the guard had not fired, the death toll would certainly have been higher," the ICRC said. "Robbery was not the aim of the attack."

The killings were the worst involving ICRC staff members in the humanitarian organisation's 133-year-old history. They are a big blow to the agency, which has lost 49 staff members in attacks in the past 10 years.

On Friday, the head of the ICRC, Cornelio Sommaruga, led 500 mourners in praising the victims slain in Chechnya for their "solidarity with the victims" of the conflict in the region at a memorial service at Geneva's Saint Peter's Cathedral.
"We are in mourning, horrified by this revolting massacre. It is the profound mourning of everyone in the humanitarian world and their friends," Sommaruga said.
"The ICRC is profundly shocked and grieved by this tragedy."

The five women medical workers and male construction manager -- from Canada, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway and Spain -- follow three Swiss staff killed in an ambush in Burundi last June and a Swiss slain on a convoy entering Sarajevo in 1992.
Their bodies were brought to Geneva on Wednesday and have been flown home since.
Sommaruga later took part in a silent march for the victims attended by nearly 1,000 humanitarian workers.
He described the careers of each, noting Gunnhild Myklebust, 55, one of two slain Norwegian Red Cross nurses, had become a grandmother while serving in Chechnya.
Fernanda Calado, a 49-year-old chief nurse from Spain, had worked for ICRC for 12 years in conflict zones including Angola, Israel, Cambodia, Somalia, and Rwanda.
"Every one of us feels deep in his or her heart the dreadful blow dealt so brutally to the victims' families on the eve of the festive season," the ICRC president said.
